claim: In retaliation for Donald Trump's border wall plan, Mexico will soon shift all its imports of corn, rice, soy, and wheat from the United States to Argentina.
label: half
explain: Two of Donald Trump’s most prominent 2016 campaign pledges were to build a border wall along the Mexican border (or rather, to reinforce and extend it; a wall already exists along hundreds of miles of the international border), and to renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement, a 1994 arrangement between the United States, Canada and Mexico which he called “the single worst trade deal ever approved in this country.”In October 2017, left-wing Facebook page “The Other 98%” posted a widely-shared meme which claimed that Mexico had — in retaliation for Trump’s border wall plans — signed a major agricultural trade agreement with Argentina, which would have very harmful effects on American farmers:As of 1 November 2017, Mexico and Argentina have not signed an agreement like the one described by “The Other 98%”, but the two countries have held talks about a more limited (though still significant) trade deal involving grains and cars. Furthermore, the main catalyst for the negotiations has been the uncertainty caused by Donald Trump’s vow to renegotiate NAFTA rather than his plans to build a border wall. The source cited by “The Other 98%” is a September 2017 article by Daily Kos, which reported:It’s not clear what the source of these claims is, but a similar meme appeared online earlier in 2017, which read:“Made in America Week” took place from 17-24 July 2017; we found no evidence of any deal between Mexico and Argentina being announced during that time period. However, talks have been ongoing between the two countries. In the spring of 2017, Mexico’s Deputy Economy Minister Juan Carlos Baker made several comments in interviews about his country’s negotiations with Argentina and Brazil. On 26 March 2017, the Financial Times reported:The following month, Baker told Reuters that a deal with Argentina could be finalized by the end of 2017:A trade deal between Mexico and Argentina may be in the works, but it has not yet been announced as of 1 November 2017. However, assuming a deal goes ahead to shift Mexico’s importation of certain products from the United States to Argentina, the numbers are significant — but not as dramatic as they are in the meme.According to United States Grain Council statistics, the United States exported $2.5 billion worth of corn to Mexico in 2015 and 2016. In 2015, the United States exported $2.9 billion worth of soy products to Mexico, according to the U.S. Soybean Export Council (page 19.) According to Global Agricultural Trade System statistics for 2016, exports of wheat and rice were worth $612 million and $274 million, respectively. This yields a total of $6.3 billion in U.S. exports to Mexico of corn, rice, wheat and soy — the four products specified in the above meme. So even if Mexico did decide to stop importing all these products from the U.S., the likely annual financial cost to the American agriculture industry would be extremely significant, but still only around half the $13 billion claimed.It’s not entirely clear where the figure of $13 billion came from, but it might have originated in an October 2017 letter sent to Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, and signed by dozens of food and agriculture companies and industry associations, warning Ross about the dangers, as they see them, of withdrawing from NAFTA. The study mentioned here was an August 2017 working paper produced by the economic consulting firm ImpactECON. It did not actually mention any figure of $13 billion. Rather, it projected that over the course of two to three years after a U.S. withdrawal from NAFTA, real GDP in the United States would fall by as much as 0.09 percent.Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the combined market value of all goods and services produced in a particular geographic area (in this case, the United States.) It is a calculation commonly used to measure the total size of an economy. Real GDP is gross domestic product adjusted for inflation – meaning, roughly speaking, the size of the economy in relation to the cost of living. As of the third quarter of 2017 (when the ImpactECON report was published), the real GDP of the United States was $17.01 trillion, according to figures from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. A 0.09 percent decline in that would amount to a $15.3 billion loss — not far off the $13 billion posited by the food and agriculture industry, in their letter. There are a couple of things to note here: firstly, the 0.09 percent decline estimated in the ImpactECON report relates to the entire U.S. economy, and not “the farm sector alone,” as mentioned in the letter.In fact, the working paper projects a very small  in production for the crops and forestry sector (0.04 percent, page 20), accompanied by a significant boost to production in the sugar sector (5.11 percent), but it also projects production declines of between one and two percent in the meat, food and livestock and fishing sectors. Secondly, this real GDP declined is projected to happen “in the next 2-3 years”, so if the meme is using the letter to Wilbur Ross as the source of its $13 billion figure, it is misrepresenting the decline as happening “annually.”

In his immigration-reform plan , the candidate list several way to force the Mexican government to pay up :
[ T ] he United States will , among other thing : impound all remittance payment derive from illegal wage ; increase fee on all temporary visa issue to Mexican CEOs and diplomat ( and if necessary cancel them ) ; increase fee on all border cross cards—of which we issue about 1 million to Mexican national each year ( a major source of visa overstays ) ; increase fee on all NAFTA worker visa from Mexico ( another major source of overstays ) ; and increase fee at port of entry to the United States from Mexico [ Tariffs and foreign aid cut be also option ] . “ If a future President Trump negotiate a large scale guest worker visa program that allow many temporary Mexican guest worker in annually and legalize most of the unauthorized immigrant in the United States , he could gain the diplomatic leverage to prompt Mexico to build a wall—or at least deploy some troop in a fancy show , ” even if the guest-worker program render Trump ’ s wall irrelevant , Nowrasteh conclude . Maybe it ’ s because Donald Trump ’ s propose wall along the U.S.-Mexican border have more than double in height over the course of his presidential campaign , theoretically soar past the Berlin Wall and Great Wall of China . Crucially , Trump have also float the idea of Mexico pay for the wall not with a government check , but through a “ tax , ” presumably in the form of new U.S. tariff on import from Mexico . ”
When I ask Rozental about the feasibility of Mexico pay for Trump ’ s wall , he challenge my hypothetical : “ From my perspective , Trump ’ s nonsense be just that—it ’ s bravado , it ’ s rhetoric , it ’ s play on fear of people in the U.S. particularly who have lose job or who feel that in one way or another the U.S. ’ s problem be the fault of everyone other than the United States , begin with Mexico but it include obviously China , and it include Japan . A nationalist backlash to Trump ’ s policy would likely emerge in Mexico , just a anti-Americanism in the region be decline with the restoration of U.S.-Cuban relation and the election of a Washington-friendly president in Argentina . ”
Trump , in a memo to The Washington Post release this week , state that block remittance would be his preferred method of compel Mexico to pay for the wall . “ We have the ability to shut down the flow of remittance to Mexico from illegal alien work in the United States , ” Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach , a Trump supporter , say in February . And why incur these cost at a time when more Mexicans be leave the United States than come into the country , and a significant number of those who be arrive be enter the U.S. legally and then overstay their visas—a problem Trump ’ s wall can ’ t solve ? “ Mexico will then have to make a choice : Either make a single payment ... to the United States to pay for the wall , or lose most of the $ 23 billion in remittance that Mexico receive every year from it national work illegally in the United States . In an economic model produce for The Washington Post , Moody ’ s assume that Trump honor his campaign promise , impose a 35-percent tariff on import from Mexico and a 45-percent tariff on import from China . Constructing Trump ’ s wall along America ’ s 2,000-mile southern border would likely constitute the large infrastructure project in the United States since Dwight Eisenhower ’ s highway system . As president , Trump would slash U.S. funding for NATO and the United Nations ; pressure Japan and South Korea to pay more for host U.S. troop and perhaps even to develop their own nuclear weapon so they ’ ll quit rely on America ’ s nuclear deterrent ; make Germany and the Gulf state provide the money for “ safe zone ” in Syria ; and coerce Saudi Arabia into “ reimburse ” the United States for protect the kingdom . Critics like Hillary Clinton may interpret his wall proposal a fantasy because Trump ’ s underlying idea be so big—because he ’ s advocate for an alternate reality in which the United States put up wall , shed alliance , and spurns free trade , and dispense with 70 year of accumulated , largely bipartisan wisdom about how America should conduct itself abroad . ”
There be good reason to treat Trump ’ s plan to build a wall on Mexico ’ s dime a the opposite of fantasy . This be what Trump appear to have in mind when he muse about “ play with ” the U.S.-Mexican trade deficit , and such action would violate the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement ( NAFTA ) , which create a largely tariff-free trade zone across the U.S. , Mexico , and Canada . Whatever the explanation , Trump ’ s critic tend to dismiss his pledge to make Mexico “ pay for the wall ” a a cheap , chauvinist applause line at best and a dangerous deception at worst—an attempt to foist an impossible dream on an impossible benefactor . The answer , when it come to Mexico , offer a case study in what Trump ’ s America-First theory might look like in practice . As president , he would propose refashion counterterrorism regulation to require that money-transfer company like Western Union ask immigrant to present their legal document before wire money outside the United States . ” In short : The Mexican government will have to choose between forsake it poor citizen or building Trump ’ s wall . “ The Mexican government and the Mexican people be totally against the idea of wall off the border , ” Andrés Rozental , a former Mexican ambassador and deputy foreign minister , tell me . “ The most beautiful tall wall , good than the Great Wall of China , that will run the whole border , that he would somehow magically get the Mexican government to pay for , ” Hillary Clinton muse in March . “ The first thing that the Mexican government have behind it position be that partner such a the U.S. and Mexico , in the North American Free Trade Agreement as well a two country that be geographically contiguous , should not and do not need wall to separate them at the border . ” The revenue that a President Trump raise from this scheme “ could go to promote security on the border , which could be a wall. Even if all these machination cause Mexico to cough up cash , the U.S. Congress would need to appropriate the money to build the wall . Mexican official will immediately protest , Trump predict , but they ’ ll probably capitulate and “ make a one-time payment of $ 5-10 billion ” to prevent the regulation from go into effect . But he ’ s give little detail about how he ’ d do this—just because Americans purchase $ 58 billion more in good and service from Mexico than Mexicans buy from the U.S. doesn ’ t mean the Mexican government itself have those fund lie around to give back to the United States . “ [ U ] ntil all of these obstacle be overcome—until funding be procure from Mexico , the Congress give it approval , and the court sign off—construction of the wall couldn ’ t even begin . ” But , a Aaron Wallen , a lecturer at Columbia Business School , recently tell Slate , Trump ’ s inflexible stance on how the wall will be finance , and the Mexican government ’ s rigid refusal to foot the bill , appear to have leave nothing in the way of what negotiator call a “ zone of possible agreement , ” or ZOPA . It will be “ an easy decision for Mexico , ” Trump claim . Trump , of course , could merely be stake out an extreme position at the outset of negotiation with Mexico—a common deal-making tactic know a “ anchoring. Trump have say he will essentially use America ’ s $ 58-billion trade deficit with Mexico a a treasure chest . Mexico , for example , might agree to subsidize the wall in return for a new trade deal with the U.S. that be favorable to Mexican interest . ”
Another reason to take it seriously : The plan be consistent with Trump ’ s extractive , neo-mercantilist worldview . ( Later that year , Eisenhower conduct mass deportation of undocumented Mexican immigrants—an operation Trump have praise . ) “ It be likely that the vote for fund construction of a border wall would be the big , most consequential , and hardest-fought since the passage of Obamacare , ” Geraghty write . As Binyamin Appelbaum note in The New York Times , when the U.S. company Carrier shift the manufacturing of it air conditioner to Mexico , that make air conditioner cheap for all Americans . Shannon O ’ Neil , a Latin America expert at the Council on Foreign Relations , tell me that while the Mexican government ’ s finance be fairly healthy relative to those in other emerge market , the government recently respond to global economic uncertainty and low oil price by reduce it 2016 budget by $ 7 billion , cut long-term investment in infrastructure project like road and bridge ( or , say , wall ) . Trump say the wall will cost no more than $ 12 billion , but some expert estimate that it could require an investment of $ 25 billion or more , not include hefty maintenance cost . Maybe it ’ s because Mexico ’ s former president say he wouldn ’ t pay for “ that fuck wall.
